summary: Defines a framework for grouping the media lines (m lines) of a Session Description Protocol (SDP) description, using the group and mid attributes. It shows two uses: lip synchronization of audio and video, and receiving one media flow made of several streams on different transport addresses. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 3388.

eli5.summary: A video call has sound and picture. This gives each part a name tag and lets you say which parts belong together, like matching a voice to the moving lips.

questions: what is the sdp mid attribute
what is the sdp group attribute
what is lip synchronization in sdp
subtitle: Name each media line in an SDP description and say which lines belong together, for lip sync or for one stream split across several addresses.

tldr.problem: An SDP description can contain several media ("m") lines, but SDP has no way to say how they relate to each other, so applications have to guess what to do with them.
tldr.mechanism: The "mid" attribute gives each "m" line a unique tag, and the session-level "group" attribute lists tags under a named semantics: LS for lip synchronization, FID for one media flow spread over several "m" lines.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3388, turns the grouping mechanism into an extensible framework, and has been updated by RFC 8843 and RFC 9143.

facts.label: Semantics token length
facts.value: SHOULD be at most four characters

today: RFC 5888 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3388 and has been updated by RFC 8843 and RFC 9143.

sections.title: Why Media Lines Need Grouping
sections.content:
A Session Description Protocol (SDP) description from RFC 4566 can contain several media lines, known as "m" lines. When it has more than one, SDP offers no way to express a relationship between them, and SDP carries no information about grouping media streams. It is left to the application to decide what to do.

Sometimes this can be carried out of band, but a mechanism inside SDP is needed. RFC 5888 provides it as a framework and obsoletes RFC 3388.
sections.eli5: If a page has several pictures and no captions, you cannot tell which ones go together. This document adds captions and a way to say which belong as a set.

sections.title: The mid and group Attributes
sections.content:
Each "m" line is identified by a token carried in a mid (media stream identification) attribute below it: a=mid: followed by an identification tag, which MUST be unique within the session description. Session-level group attributes then list tags: a=group: followed by a semantics value and zero or more identification tags.

The semantics says what the group is for. Two are defined here, LS and FID. New semantics follow the Standards Action policy of RFC 5226. The formats are written in ABNF.

If any "m" line has no "mid", the application MUST NOT group media lines at all. Every "m" line must carry a "mid" whether or not it appears in a group. A "group" line naming a tag that matches no "m" line MUST be ignored. A description MAY hold several "group" lines, with the same or different semantics, and an "m" line MAY appear in more than one.
sections.eli5: Every picture gets a name tag. Then a list at the top says things like 'pictures 1 and 2 go together'. If any picture has no tag, you ignore the lists.

sections.title: Lip Synchronization (LS)
sections.content:
An application that receives "m" lines grouped with LS semantics MUST synchronize the playout of those streams. This is not only for video with audio; two streams of the same type can be synchronized too.

For RTP streams, synchronization is typically done with RTCP, which gives enough information to map the time stamps of different streams to a local absolute time. For streams that do not use RTP, the application MUST recover the original timing relationship using whatever mechanism is available.

The RFC's example is a multicast conference with English speech (mid 1), video (mid 2) and a Spanish translation (mid 3). Only 1 and 2 are grouped with a=group:LS 1 2. The third stream is left out of the group but still carries its own "mid".
sections.eli5: When a movie is playing, the voice must match the lips. LS tells the player to keep these two streams in step.

sections.title: Flow Identification (FID)
sections.content:
The RFC argues that one media instance can use more than one RTP session. Examples are cellular systems with a separate radio bearer, and so a separate port, per codec, and a voice session whose DTMF tones are handled by a different host. So it defines a media flow: a single media instance which, when RTP is used, comprises one or more RTP sessions.

"m" lines grouped with FID form one media flow. The media agent encodes with one codec at a time and checks the lines one by one. For each line that lists the current codec and whose direction is sendonly or sendrecv, it MUST send a copy to that line's address and port. Other lines get nothing. So the destination typically changes as the codec changes.

In the RFC's examples, GSM goes to port 30000 and AMR to port 30002, PCM goes to a transcoder at 192.0.2.2 while AMR goes to the terminal, and voice and DTMF telephone events go to two different addresses.

FID MUST NOT be used for parallel encodings of the same information with different codecs at once, such as DTMF sent both as voice and as telephone events, nor for the layers of a layered encoding. It MUST NOT group "m" lines with the same IP address and port; those must be one "m" line listing several codecs. FID-grouped lines MUST differ in their transport addresses.
sections.eli5: Imagine one speaker who can talk in several languages, with a different mailbox for each language. FID lists the mailboxes, and you post to the one that matches the language you are using.

sections.title: Using group in SIP Offers and Answers
sections.content:
Using SIP (RFC 3261) with the offer/answer model of RFC 3264, the "mid" in an answer MUST match the offer, and later offers SHOULD reuse it. Media alignment still follows the nth "m" line rule regardless of "group" or "mid". If a stream has a different "mid" in the answer, all "mid" and "group" lines are ignored.

An answerer that does not understand a group's semantics MUST answer without the "group" line, but keep the "mid" lines. One that does understand MUST return a "group" line with the same semantics and the same tags or a subset. A refused stream has its port set to zero and MUST NOT appear in a "group" line. Grouping MUST be requested by the offerer, never the answerer, because the answerer could not know whether the offerer accepted it. An answerer that wants grouping sends a new offer, for instance in a re-INVITE.

A client can show it supports a semantics without using it by adding an empty line such as a=group:FID. A server SHOULD answer with its own empty lines. If the answerer does not understand "group", it ignores it; it may then mix the streams or reject the request, for example with 488 or 606, and the client can retry with one "m" line per flow.
sections.eli5: The person who asks makes the list. The person who answers either agrees to the same list, crosses off items, or says 'I do not know that kind of list'.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3388
sections.content:
The overview section was added, acronyms such as AMR and GSM are expanded, and the examples use IP addresses reserved for examples. The grouping mechanism is now an extensible framework, whereas RFC 3388 discouraged extensions in favor of new session description protocols.

RFC 3388 also limited an "m" line identifier to one group per semantics. That restriction is lifted. The RFC argues this causes no backward-compatibility problems, since legacy implementations only enforce it for the semantics they support.
sections.eli5: The rules got a clearer introduction, and now a picture may belong to more than one list.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
With FID, someone who can modify the exchanged session descriptions could make participants send a copy of the media to any destination. Integrity protection on the exchange and media encryption can prevent this. For SIP, S/MIME and TLS can protect the exchange end to end and hop by hop.

IANA registers the "mid" and "group" attributes and a registry of semantics under Standards Action. Each entry needs a description, a token that SHOULD be no more than four characters, and a standards track reference. Current entries include LS, FID, SRF (RFC 3524) and ANAT (RFC 4091), plus FEC and DDP.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person who changes the list could make your video be mailed to them too, so the list should be protected.

viz.caption: FID EXAMPLE FROM THE RFC: GSM AND AMR ON TWO PORTS

data.title: Two codecs, one media flow
data.code:
v=0
o=Laura 289083124 289083124 IN IP4 three.example.com
c=IN IP4 192.0.2.1
t=0 0
a=group:FID 1 2
m=audio 30000 RTP/AVP 3
a=rtpmap:3 GSM/8000
a=mid:1
m=audio 30002 RTP/AVP 97
a=rtpmap:97 AMR/8000
a=mid:2
